searchText: The subgroup check avoids small subgroup attacks which would allow people impersonating a private key. - https://jonasnick.github.io/blog/2017/05/23/exploiting-low-order-generators-in-one-time-ring-signatures/ - https://www.getmonero.org/ru/2017/05/17/disclosure-of-a-major-bug-in-cryptonote-based-currencies.html - https://loup-vaillant.fr/tutorials/cofactor But this is a user concern, isn't it? Or a smart contract actually need to know the inputs are not from a small subgroup or otherwise it cannot trust the proof. User's key are using secp256k1. There are no user keys on BN254 G1 or G2. BN254 G1 has no cofactor, so the only potential issue is for G2. Then the question becomes, can a smart contract use the lack of subgroup checks to break pairings. I have no cryptographic answer, but I know from debugging that if you're not in the correct subgroup, you get wrong result anytime you use an endomorphism. And pairings use the "twist-frobenius endomorphism-twist" for efficiency. Now regarding the question, is it possible to generate D not in the subgroup, Yes. But you should not start the random point by multiplying with the generator point. Instead you should start from a random x coordinate, then compute `x³ + 3/(9+i)` and then take the square root. This will give you (x, y) coordinates on the E2 curve (the "full group") You can check if that point is in the subgroup with: https://github.com/mratsim/constantine/blob/master/constantine/math/constants/bn254_snarks_subgroups.nim#L191-L217 ```Nim func isInSubgroup*(P: ECP_ShortW_Jac[Fp2[BN254_Snarks], G2] or ECP_ShortW_Prj[Fp2[BN254_Snarks], G2]): SecretBool = ## Returns true if P is in G2 subgroup, i.e. P is a point of order r. ## A point may be on a curve but not on the prime order r subgroup. ## Not checking subgroup exposes a protocol to small subgroup attacks. # Implementation: Scott, https://eprint.iacr.org/2021/1130.pdf # A note on group membership tests for G1, G2 and GT # on BLS pairing-friendly curves # # The condition to apply the optimized endomorphism check on G₂ # is gcd(h₁, h₂) == 1 with h₁ and h₂ the cofactors on G₁ and G₂. # In that case [p]Q == [t-1]Q as r = p+1-t and [r]Q = 0 # For BN curves h₁ = 1, hence Scott group membership tests can be used for BN curves # # p the prime modulus: 36u⁴ + 36u³ + 24u² + 6u + 1 # r the prime order: 36u⁴ + 36u³ + 18u² + 6u + 1 # t the trace: 6u² + 1 var t0{.noInit.}, t1{.noInit.}: typeof(P) t0.pow_bn254_snarks_u(P) # [u]P t1.pow_bn254_snarks_u(t0) # [u²]P t0.double(t1) # [2u²]P t0 += t1 # [3u²]P t0.double() # [6u²]P t1.frobenius_psi(P) # ψ(P) return t0 == t1 ``` In my experience, it's very likely to get a point out of the subgroup. oh actually my comment confirms that you can't use endomorphisms except if in the proper subgroup ^ Thanks, I already did this.

excerpts.content: But this is a user concern, isn't it? Or a smart contract actually need to know the inputs are not from a small subgroup or otherwise it cannot trust the proof.

excerpts.author: mratsim
excerpts.content:
User's key are using secp256k1.
There are no user keys on BN254 G1 or G2.

BN254 G1 has no cofactor, so the only potential issue is for G2.
Then the question becomes, can a smart contract use the lack of subgroup checks to break pairings.

I have no cryptographic answer, but I know from debugging that if you're not in the correct subgroup, you get wrong result anytime you use an endomorphism.
And pairings use the "twist-frobenius endomorphism-twist" for efficiency.

excerpts.author: mratsim
excerpts.content:
Now regarding the question, is it possible to generate D not in the subgroup,

Yes.

But you should not start the random point by multiplying with the generator point.

Instead you should start from a random x coordinate, then compute `x³ + 3/(9+i)` and then take the square root.

excerpts.author: mratsim
excerpts.content:
You can check if that point is in the subgroup with: https://github.com/mratsim/constantine/blob/master/constantine/math/constants/bn254_snarks_subgroups.nim#L191-L217

```Nim
func isInSubgroup*(P: ECP_ShortW_Jac[Fp2[BN254_Snarks], G2] or ECP_ShortW_Prj[Fp2[BN254_Snarks], G2]): SecretBool =
  ## Returns true if P is in G2 subgroup, i.e. P is a point of order r.
  ## A point may be on a curve but not on the prime order r subgroup.
  ## Not checking subgroup exposes a protocol to small subgroup attacks.
  # Implementation: Scott, https://eprint.iacr.org/2021/1130.pdf
  #   A note on group membership tests for G1, G2 and GT
  #   on BLS pairing-friendly curves
  #
  #   The condition to apply the optimized endomorphism check on G₂ 
  #   is gcd(h₁, h₂) == 1 with h₁ and h₂ the cofactors on G₁ and G₂.
  #   In that case [p]Q == [t-1]Q as r = p+1-t and [r]Q = 0
  #   For BN curves h₁ = 1, hence Scott group membership tests can be used for BN curves
  #   
  #   p the prime modulus: 36u⁴ + 36u³ + 24u² + 6u + 1
  #   r the prime order:   36u⁴ + 36u³ + 18u² + 6u + 1
  #   t the trace:         6u² + 1
  var t0{.noInit.}, t1{.noInit.}: typeof(P)
  
  t0.pow_bn254_snarks_u(P)  # [u]P
  t1.pow_bn254_snarks_u(t0) # [u²]P
  t0.double(t1)             # [2u²]P
  t0 += t1                  # [3u²]P
  t0.double()               # [6u²]P
  
  t1.frobenius_psi(P)       # ψ(P)

  return t0 == t1
```
